title: Non-Destructive Radiocaesium Screening of Intact Wild Game Meat: Screening-Level Calibration and Measurement-Error Structure
content: Japan's official non-destructive radiocaesium screening method allows food-specific screening levels (SL) to be set by linear regression against reference germanium (Ge) spectrometry. It does not cover wild game meat, in which concentrations above the 100 Bq kg−1 standard limit are still found in Fukushima Prefecture. We evaluated this regression-based approach with intact quadriceps femoris muscle blocks from 126 wild animals (wild boar, Asian black bear, and sika deer), measured unfrozen and/or frozen with commercial CsI(Tl) and NaI(Tl) instruments. SL point estimates ranged from 43.2 to 81.1 Bq kg−1 in all eight strata, meeting the requirement of SL ≥ 25 Bq kg−1, although one lower bootstrap confidence limit was 25.4 Bq kg−1. No sample exceeding the standard limit was screened negative in the primary or leave-one-out evaluation. The upper 95% confidence limits of the false-negative rate were 6.7% (frozen) and 10.0% (unfrozen) for wild boar. For bear and deer, with only 4 and 5 exceeding samples, they were 60.2% and 52.2%. Residual variance increased with concentration in most strata and was dominated by sample-specific deviations rather than replicate variation. Under a fitted variance-function model, the model-based miss probability at 100 Bq kg−1 was 0.10%–0.43% for wild boar, but was higher (1.26%–4.60%) and model-dependent for bear and deer. Paired measurements showed that frozen wild boar blocks gave lower indications than unfrozen blocks. Although the SL requirement was met, the implied false-negative control depended on the concentration-dependent error structure and the calibration data.
